name: USB

claims.claim_text: USB 1.0 ran at 1.5 megabits per second and USB 1.1 at 12 megabits per second; USB 2 raised this to rates comparable with FireWire.
claims.quote_verbatim: USB 1.0 was 1.5 megabits per second. I was right. And then USB 1.1 is 12 megabits per second
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: USB is a multi-drop bus, which is why the contemporaneous FireWire standard retained advantages in data synchronisation and sustained throughput even after USB matched it on headline rate.
claims.quote_verbatim: USB is like a multi-drop standard. And it's like, it's not as good for, you know, high speed transfer as 1394 was
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A device's speed grade is signalled by pull-up and pull-down resistors on the data lines and is established when the host first sees the device, rather than being negotiated in software after defaulting to the slowest rate.
claims.quote_verbatim: based on like pull-ups and pull-down resistors on different lines
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A low- or full-speed USB receiver decodes the differential pair into a small number of line states, the J and K states plus both-low, with both-high an error condition that should not occur; that is enough to implement the protocol without dedicated hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: you detect, uh, all four state possible
claims.speaker: Sylvain Munaut

claims.claim_text: High-speed USB at 480 megabits per second requires a true differential receiver and an external PHY, typically over a ULPI interface that deserialises the line into a parallel bus; it cannot be done on ordinary logic pins.
claims.quote_verbatim: there you need true differential receiver and you need also a five because I mean 480 megabits
claims.speaker: Sylvain Munaut

claims.claim_text: Implementing USB 3 requires gigabit serial transceivers with clock recovery, which is why at that speed dedicated hardware rather than fabric logic becomes necessary.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need to do the clock recovery as well
claims.speaker: Sylvain Munaut

claims.claim_text: A USB 3 PHY that must also support USB 2 hosts carries the older ULPI interface alongside a 32-bit data bus, reaching seventy or eighty pins in total; backwards compatibility, not the new protocol, accounts for much of that pin count.
claims.quote_verbatim: partly the reason it has a lot of pins is for backwards compatibility with the, the ULPI interface for USB 2.0
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: Every layer of USB remains backwards compatible with the two-wire USB 2.0 signalling beneath it, with the additional capabilities negotiated at connection time; alternate modes and power delivery are layered on top of that base.
claims.quote_verbatim: everything's backwards compatible to the slowest thing

claims.claim_text: USB was designed to move data cheaply and reliably, but not to move it reliably against a deadline, which is the requirement a streaming instrument has.
claims.quote_verbatim: moving data reliably with a deadline is not something that it's ever done that great

claims.claim_text: USB offers four transfer types with different guarantees: control for basic device communication, interrupt for periodic small transfers such as a mouse, bulk for guaranteed delivery without guaranteed bandwidth as used by mass storage, and isochronous for dedicated bandwidth without retry. Neither bulk nor isochronous gives both guaranteed bandwidth and guaranteed delivery, which is the combination a continuous instrument needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: The problem with isochronous is if you lose something, you lose it. The problem with bulk is if you lose something, it's going to retry

claims.claim_text: Streaming over USB is workable in practice provided the design stays well below the bus's capacity and does not compete with other high-bandwidth devices on the same controller.
claims.quote_verbatim: as long as you follow some basic guidelines and don't put too much bandwidth over your USB bus, then you'll be okay

claims.claim_text: In a software radio built around a host connection, the maximum rate of high-speed USB sets the sample rate and therefore the instantaneous bandwidth of the whole instrument: a pair of eight-bit quadrature samples 20 million times per second saturates the link, giving 20 MHz of bandwidth.
claims.quote_verbatim: my primary limitation and the limitation that hacker one is designed around is the, the maximum speed of high speed USB
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: That USB-imposed ceiling turned out to be a well-matched design point, because analog and digital parts capable of substantially more than 20 megasamples per second rise steeply in price, while the resulting bandwidth is many times what a low-cost tuner dongle provides.
claims.quote_verbatim: finding components that would really do the job much faster than that, end up being a lot more expensive
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: Where the host connection is the bottleneck, on-board signal processing can be omitted entirely: a small CPLD for glue logic and a microcontroller with a built-in high-speed USB interface are enough to get samples in and out, leaving the processing to the host.
claims.quote_verbatim: one way I was able to reduce costs and power consumption is just to go without an FPGA
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: A whole class of USB-connected instruments, including logic analysers and current measurement instruments, follows the same architecture of shipping raw data to the host and doing all analysis there, in place of the embedded computer a traditional bench instrument contains.
claims.quote_verbatim: They just ship all the data back over to the host computer and do whatever they need to over there

claims.claim_text: Instruments whose content is a front end plus a converter, such as dynamic signal analysers, have largely been replaced by headless USB boxes, because the front panel, processor and display duplicate what the attached computer already provides.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've been replaced by boxes that hook onto your USB port now
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Specialized and/or Open Source Test Gear and Dev Boards - Vacation Videography Vorboten

claims.claim_text: A USB 2 port supplies 500 milliamps, about two and a half watts, and ports on a machine typically share one controller, so a product that must work in any port has to be specified against that lowest common denominator rather than against a favourable case.
claims.quote_verbatim: usb is it's 500 max on a single controller
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Hyperloop, Upverter and Soldering - Unbelievable USB Ustulater

claims.claim_text: The original 500 milliamp limit was advisory rather than enforced: hosts supplied the current regardless, and requesting a smaller budget only mattered for leaving headroom for other devices. In practice designers wired devices to the 5 volt rail and ignored the negotiation, because policing it would have meant disconnecting devices.
claims.quote_verbatim: all the devices were just capable of providing 500 milliamps anyway
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: USB-C power negotiation begins with the source holding pull-ups on both CC lines; a voltage drop on one of them indicates both that a plug is present and which orientation it is in, after which 5 volts appears on VBUS. A capable source then broadcasts its available voltage and current combinations, the sink requests one by index, and the source grants it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's monitoring both of the CC lines. There's CC1 and CC2. And it'll activate pull-ups on those lines
claims.speaker: Jason Cerundolo

claims.claim_text: A multi-port source must track its total input power against everything it has already promised, since granting every port its full allocation would require a supply many times the size of any single port's rating.
claims.quote_verbatim: it has to keep track of what's its total input power, and then how much is it promised to each of the ports
claims.speaker: Jason Cerundolo

claims.claim_text: Drawing more than the default current from a USB-C source does not require a power delivery controller. A pull-down on the CC pin and a reading of that pin's voltage with an ordinary microcontroller analog input distinguishes the 500 milliamp, 1.5 amp and 3 amp advertisements; full power delivery messaging is needed only beyond that.
claims.quote_verbatim: you basically just need, uh, an ADC, which you probably already have on your microcontroller
claims.speaker: Jason Cerundolo

claims.claim_text: Galvanic isolation is straightforward on USB-A, where the cable carries only ground, VBUS and the two data lines and VBUS is always present, and much harder on USB-C, where an ideal source holds VBUS at zero until a 5.1 kilohm pull-down on a CC pin signals an attached device, and then superimposes digital messaging on that same line.
claims.quote_verbatim: with a USB-A, a regular USB 2.0 USB-A cable, it's four pins plus a shield
claims.episode_title: Software Defined Power Supplies with Werner Johansson

claims.claim_text: Convergence on a single charging connector across mobile phones was achieved by legislation mandating it, not by market pressure.
claims.quote_verbatim: all new mobile phones must use a USB for charging
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The USB core is a significant contributor to a system-on-module's idle power, enough that on one compute module it is left disabled in the default device tree and must be deliberately enabled.
claims.quote_verbatim: USB is one of the ones that really sucks down a lot of the power

claims.claim_text: A single-board computer's downstream USB ports may not supply enough current for two power-hungry peripherals such as Wi-Fi adapters, and the symptom appears as unreliable operation rather than as an explicit power fault.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Raspberry Pi like doesn't give enough juice to the USB ports
claims.speaker: Samy Kamkar

claims.claim_text: Bulk decoupling capacitance downstream of a USB protection device draws an inrush at insertion that can trip the protection into overcurrent shutdown. The same fault has also been observed with nothing plugged in, correlating with several hundred millivolts of noise on the 5 volt rail, indicating the protection chip can be triggered by supply noise as well as by real overcurrent.
claims.quote_verbatim: they were taking a surge of current to charge the bulk capacitors. And that was causing the chip to go into overcurrent mode
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Connecting a mains-earthed USB host to equipment running from a floating supply creates a ground path through the USB cable, and the resulting problems appear even though the interface itself carries little power.
claims.quote_verbatim: as soon as you plug a USB, grounded USB, Earth mains grounded USB, to a device with floating wall plug, you get problems

claims.claim_text: A digital isolator in the USB path, commonly a capacitive rather than optical part, is standard practice when debugging equipment at elevated potential, because otherwise the host computer's ground becomes the reference for whatever the equipment is connected to.
claims.quote_verbatim: usually I'll do like USB isolators

claims.claim_text: High-speed USB and HDMI can be routed successfully on a two-layer board provided the connector is placed close to the controller; the short controlled length matters more than layer count.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can do high-speed USB and HDMI on a two-layer board, for goodness sake
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: USB signalling is pseudo-differential, swinging between zero and the supply rather than symmetrically about zero, so the crossover between the two lines is not exact. The resulting skew produces a common-mode spike at every transition, which is why common-mode chokes on USB pairs are an effective emissions measure.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's pseudo differential. It's not true differential. It doesn't go around zero volts
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: In a product failing radiated emissions, a week of work filtering the custom boards found nothing; the source was a cheaply sourced USB hub bearing full compliance markings. A bought-in module's emissions profile is not knowable from its certification, since it was tested in a different configuration of cables and boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's what the failure came back to
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: USB 3 will refuse to negotiate a link if the signal pairs are broken out to test pads or branched at all, so the debugging convenience of accessible test points is unavailable at super-speed.
claims.quote_verbatim: I cannot get a USB 3 link to establish if I have any breakouts at all. I can't have any branching

claims.claim_text: Inserting any instrument in series with a super-speed bus degrades the signalling unless the interposer includes a repeater.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you start talking about interrupting a super speed bus, that signaling gets a little dodgy unless you have a repeater

claims.claim_text: A product operating at the limit of its link budget fails intermittently once an adapter and an internal ribbon cable are added in series, and works when connected directly; the fault is cumulative margin loss, not any single defective element.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're on the edge of what they can do, data rate for the USB-C connection
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Wow, Dave REALLY likes Top Gun

claims.claim_text: USB data pairs are routed to a differential impedance of about 90 ohms, distinct from the impedance targets of other high-speed interfaces on the same board.
claims.quote_verbatim: USB is 90 ohm, right? The controlled impedance

claims.claim_text: Porting an existing USB stack to a new architecture is generally preferred over writing one, both because supporting the full set of device and host classes is a large undertaking and because a shared implementation means bug fixes flow in both directions between the teams using it.
claims.quote_verbatim: USB is a pretty hefty protocol stack
claims.speaker: Trey German
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Trey German - Launchpad Laden Lodesman

claims.claim_text: Implementing USB properly in a small commercial product consumed months of engineering, working through device classes, descriptors, string descriptors and composite devices before any of the product's own functionality was exercised.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like don't ask how long David too has been working on implementing the USB stuff for the micro supply
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A vendor USB stack supplied under a licence that forbids redistributing the source forces an open project to strip that code out before publishing, breaking a one-click build for anyone trying to learn from the project. A community-contributed open stack replaced it and additionally offered features, such as double buffering, that the vendor library lacked.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can use it freely, but you can't actually include the source when you distribute it
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Replacing a fixed-function USB-to-serial chip with a microcontroller running an open-source USB stack turns the interface into something reprogrammable through an on-board programming header, at the cost of having to maintain firmware for it.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've essentially taken a proprietary USB-to-serial IC, and they've replaced it with something which is an AVR, which is actually running an open-source USB-to-serial stack

claims.claim_text: Microcontroller USB stacks are mature on the device side and thin on the host side: a common open stack handles keyboards, mice and some audio devices as a host, and supporting anything further means porting the equivalent Linux driver, which is why most microcontroller designs act as devices.
claims.quote_verbatim: the device side of it is very well supported. But the host side is very basic
claims.speaker: Liam Fraser
claims.episode_title: Embedded Hardware with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Programmable IO blocks that handle bit-level serial protocols reach their limit with USB, because the protocol's response deadlines leave no room for the software half of the split between hardware bit-banging and firmware processing.
claims.quote_verbatim: something like USB where you have very tight bounds on the responses
claims.speaker: Luke Wren
claims.episode_title: Embedded Hardware with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Unless a product needs the data rate, presenting it as a serial port over a USB-to-serial bridge is the better engineering choice, because a native USB device requires custom host software while a virtual serial port can be driven from any terminal program the customer already has.
claims.quote_verbatim: unless your product needs the data rate, you're actually better off just using an FT-232 chip and converting it to serial
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Any microcontroller with a USB peripheral can be made into a USB-to-serial bridge in firmware, which sets a ceiling on what a dedicated bridge chip can be worth.
claims.quote_verbatim: Any USB capable micro can be turned into a USB to UART bridge
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Some fixed-function USB-to-serial parts are ordinary microcontrollers from the same vendor's catalogue shipped with firmware programmed in, sold as a separate product with its own datasheet and support.
claims.quote_verbatim: Their new MCP2200 USB to serial chip, which they advertise as, you know, on their website is just a USB to serial chip
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Agilent, Analog, Cold Fusion - Funding Fusion Is Not Futile

claims.claim_text: USB imposes a clock accuracy requirement that a free-running internal oscillator does not meet. Some microcontrollers close the gap by trimming their internal oscillator against the synchronisation packets on the bus, an option not available on FPGAs, which therefore need an external crystal for a USB interface.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need a certain amount of accuracy for USB
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: Handling USB communication is awkward on an FPGA and routine on a microcontroller with a built-in PHY, so designs that need both custom logic and a host connection commonly carry an FPGA and a microcontroller together.
claims.quote_verbatim: FPGAs tend not to be very good at doing stuff like, uh, handling USB comms
claims.speaker: Leigh Brady

claims.claim_text: The usual assumption that USB requires dedicated silicon, licensed as a hard core with its own PHY, is not absolute: a device with an embedded FPGA but no USB hard core has driven its USB connector directly from FPGA fabric pins.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've actually implemented a soft USB core in the FPGA
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: Low-speed USB can be bit-banged in software on a microcontroller with no USB peripheral by timing bus samples against the core clock, in one case reading or writing a bit every 53.3 cycles at 160 MHz.
claims.quote_verbatim: every 53.333 cycles, don't worry about how that works. You go either write or read a bit on the USB bus

claims.claim_text: A bit-banged USB implementation that computes the CRC and classifies the packet type inline as bits arrive can answer a host request with data immediately, where common stacks first send a negative acknowledgement, hand off to user code and reply on a later transaction.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's going to compute the polynomial for the CRC in line while it's receiving the messages

claims.claim_text: The cost of a bit-banged interface is that the processor is fully occupied during every frame it sends or receives, so the technique suits parts where a second core or a hardware peripheral is not available at the price.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you do low speed bit bang USB, it really is painful because it means that while you're sending and receiving frames, you can't be doing other stuff

claims.claim_text: Software USB on a ten-cent microcontroller changes what is worth building, since the alternatives with hardware USB were parts at roughly 70 cents to a dollar forty. The same vendor later offered a variant with hardware USB at around four times the price of the base part.
claims.quote_verbatim: This is 10 cents. You have no excuse for just putting into something

claims.claim_text: Presenting a development board as a mass-storage device removes the toolchain from the edit-run loop entirely: the file is edited in any text editor and saved, and the board runs it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you plug it into your computer and it will show up as a USB drive
claims.speaker: Scott Shawcroft

claims.claim_text: Firmware update over USB has standard classes to build on, DFU for low-level updates and mass storage for file-level access, so a device can be updated without any host-side software specific to it.
claims.quote_verbatim: There are USB protocols that are, like, standardized. So you have DFU for the low-level stuff
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg

claims.claim_text: When USB was released in 1996 the interface chips were expensive and hard for individuals to obtain, and using one meant adding a microcontroller and its software to a product; enumeration and the stack are now built into commodity microcontrollers, some of which ship with a USB bootloader already programmed.
claims.quote_verbatim: who the hell was. You know. Your average hobbyist midnight engineer. Wouldn't be able to get a USB chip in 1996
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A USB bootloader serves as the recovery path when a firmware update leaves a device unbootable, provided the bootloader itself is not what was overwritten.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can still program it over USB
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vic Aprea - Federated Firmware Functionalism

claims.claim_text: A host assigns a new virtual serial port number to each newly seen USB device and the numbering increments and eventually wraps. In a manufacturing setting where many devices are plugged in successively, this behaviour is easy to bypass during test development and to be bitten by in production.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you plug in a USB device, basically it assigns it a COM port
claims.episode_title: Wrong Hardware, Wrong Software - Fugacious Fan Funding

claims.claim_text: Host-side chipset defects have made whole classes of motherboards periodically reset every USB port, disconnecting and re-enumerating attached devices for seconds at a time; a peripheral that appears to misbehave may be reacting to this.
claims.quote_verbatim: all of the built-in USBs on the motherboard, these motherboard, AMD motherboards would like spontaneously like reset every couple of minutes
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Running a vendor toolchain inside a virtual machine and passing the USB device through to it is the common way to reconcile a toolchain that only supports one operating system with a host running another; the passthrough itself is reliable, and per-project virtual machines also preserve a working environment against later host changes.
claims.quote_verbatim: I just pass through whatever USB cable I'm plugging into that

claims.claim_text: Compatibility layers that run a Linux userspace inside another operating system generally handle files and terminals but historically could not reach the USB device, which is precisely what embedded work requires.
claims.quote_verbatim: actually talking to the hardware, you know, there's a USB port somewhere

claims.claim_text: Browser-hosted development environments can compile and simulate but cannot reach a USB device on the user's desk, which is the boundary that keeps embedded work off fully cloud-hosted toolchains.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's no way to get out to USB to actually talk to the device on your desk

claims.claim_text: USB traffic can be captured with the operating system's own monitoring facilities and written out as a packet capture, including for a guest operating system running in a virtual machine on a host that supports it, which avoids the cost of a hardware analyser.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can use the Linux kernel's USB monitoring solution
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching with Michael Ossmann and Dmitry Nedospazov

claims.claim_text: Commercial USB protocol analysers cost thousands of dollars and come with correspondingly complex software, and analysing USB 3 is substantially harder than USB 2, so most such instruments cover only up to high speed.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've got a USB analyzer and it's, yeah, it's thousands of dollars worth
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: An in-line analyser sits between host and device, passing traffic through while reading it, and a device that can also modify packets in transit becomes a fault-injection tool rather than only an observer.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's basically you're talking to one side of this thing. It's passing the packet through, but also reading it

claims.claim_text: A board with a USB device interface on each end, one facing a controlling computer and one facing a target host, allows the target's USB stack to be probed with arbitrary device behaviour; the technique has produced a large number of USB stack defects.
claims.quote_verbatim: it allows you to do things like, um, explore, uh, the security of the
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching with Michael Ossmann and Dmitry Nedospazov

claims.claim_text: The standard USB attack presents the device as a keyboard, or another human interface device, and types a stored script, so it requires no vulnerability at all: the host is behaving exactly as specified.
claims.quote_verbatim: it presents itself to the computer, typically as a keyboard
claims.speaker: Mike Grover

claims.claim_text: Such an implant fits inside the moulding of a USB-A plug on a sacrificed cable, so the visual inspection that distinguishes a suspect thumb drive from a normal one does not apply to cables.
claims.quote_verbatim: I am putting the assembled boards inside of the cables
claims.speaker: Mike Grover

claims.claim_text: A device that charges capacitors to a couple of hundred volts from the port's own 5 volt supply and discharges them into the data lines destroys the host, which argues against exposing USB ports on unattended public-facing equipment and for fast transient suppression on those that must exist.
claims.quote_verbatim: it uh buck boosts up a couple capacitors charges up to 200 volts

claims.claim_text: Removable USB storage is the standard mechanism by which malware crosses an air gap into networks that have no external connection.
claims.quote_verbatim: someone had to load it from a USB stick onto this thing because there was no internet connection
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Military Electronics and The Free Eagle (Freagle) Campaign

claims.claim_text: Firmware that sends back a buffer over USB is a memory disclosure path: corrupting the length field can make the device continue reading past the buffer and return the firmware itself if the address map places it adjacently.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you corrupt how much to send, it can actually cause it to just continue to read memory
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Shouting at chips with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: Emulating a hub and making devices appear and disappear at controlled moments is an established technique against host USB implementations, and its practicality depends on having development tools that allow the sequence to be iterated quickly.
claims.quote_verbatim: creating a USB hub and then making devices appear and disappear in order to corrupt memory

claims.claim_text: Physically identical USB-C cables differ in whether ground is bonded to the shield, whether they meet USB 2 or USB 3.2 signalling, and what identification resistor or marker chip they contain, so cable capability cannot be inferred from the connector and is worth testing.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're all bloody different. But, you know, they've all got standard USB-C connectors on them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Converging USB and Thunderbolt onto one connector was intended to reduce the number of cables in circulation but produced a set of visually indistinguishable variants supporting different combinations of USB, DisplayPort and Thunderbolt.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's specific USB-C Thunderbolt cables that don't necessarily work the same as others

claims.claim_text: USB has accumulated capability rather than replacing it: a current design must support the ubiquitous legacy USB 2 behaviour, the newer high-speed modes, and the additional dimension that USB-C and its alternate modes introduce. Choosing wrongly among those options constrains or kills a product.
claims.quote_verbatim: over time, it's sort of gotten more and more complicated because they've added alternate modes
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: USB-A contacts slide past one another rather than being pins and sockets, so the connectors have no gender in the contact sense; nor does plug and receptacle distinguish them, since extension cables exist. What distinguishes them is shrouding.
claims.quote_verbatim: they are not pins. They are not socket. They just slide past each other. So they are neither male nor female
claims.episode_title: All the Connectors with Davide Andrea

claims.claim_text: A single universal connector is impossible rather than merely unachieved: current-carrying capacity rules USB out for vehicle charging and its lack of controlled high-frequency impedance rules it out for antenna connections, so multiple connector families remain necessary.
claims.quote_verbatim: we couldn't charge our car with a USB connector because it doesn't carry enough current
claims.episode_title: All the Connectors with Davide Andrea

claims.claim_text: USB's development by an international consortium rather than a single national body is why the same connector is found everywhere, in contrast to connector families that varied by country.
claims.quote_verbatim: USB was developed by an international consortium
claims.episode_title: All the Connectors with Davide Andrea

claims.claim_text: Manufacturers formerly fitted proprietary connectors that combined USB with video and audio on a single shared interface; the practice has largely stopped, but it leaves equipment that cannot be connected without its original cable.
claims.quote_verbatim: every camera had a different freaking
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: USB-A persists in equipment such as label printers and older instruments precisely because its four-contact construction is mechanically robust and functionally sufficient.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's just D plus, D minus and a five volt and a ground

claims.claim_text: Some USB-C multiplexer and charging controllers are not sold through distribution at all and the manufacturer will not supply them to third parties, so the parts that select between USB 2, USB 3, DisplayPort and charging on a given port cannot be obtained for repair.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is a USB-C MUX chip
claims.speaker: Louis Rossmann
claims.episode_title: Right To Repair with Louis Rossmann

claims.claim_text: USB is a poor choice for sensor connections on mobile robots, where connector retention, sealing and cable robustness matter; power over Ethernet is preferred there, while USB remains well suited to automated test of embedded electronics.
claims.quote_verbatim: USB is not appropriate for mobile robots

claims.claim_text: Commodity USB hubs omit per-port power monitoring and the ability to power-cycle or disconnect a downstream device, because a dollar of monitoring silicon is not viable in a five-dollar bill of materials. Adding it lets a system identify the port whose current has jumped and disable it before the whole bus is brought down.
claims.quote_verbatim: most USB hubs don't have any diagnostic or, uh, capability or reporting don't have power monitoring

claims.claim_text: Modules intended for robotics are offered in variants that replace the USB host connection with self-booting from on-board flash or with power over Ethernet, because the mechanical and serviceability properties of the interface, not its bandwidth, decide the choice.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of times the physical, uh, nature of the robots, uh, they do not want anything to do with USB
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: Powering a teaching platform entirely from a laptop's USB port removes the need for bench power and mains distribution, which is what allows laboratory work to leave the timetabled laboratory slot.
claims.quote_verbatim: low enough power that they could power it from a USB drive for, or a USB port for 50 minutes or two hours
claims.speaker: Brock LaMeres

claims.claim_text: Development board conventions commonly bring USB 5 volts to the header through a series protection diode so that an attached board cannot back-power the host port. The consequences are that the nominal 5 volt pin sits nearer 4.4 volts and that the board cannot be powered from that pin.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's actually behind the diode, right? So that's so that you don't back power the USB port

claims.claim_text: A battery-powered design that works while plugged in and fails on battery may be depending on the host-supplied 5 volt rail for a peripheral, with the failure appearing as a firmware hang waiting for that peripheral rather than as a power fault.
claims.quote_verbatim: when it's not plugged into USB, there's no five volts that gets passed through to the particulate sensor

claims.claim_text: A USB port added for low-latency, interference-free communication also becomes the debugging and manufacturing-test interface, because it is the one connection every test computer already has and many units can be attached at once without contending for a shared channel.
claims.quote_verbatim: USB is also super useful for a lot of other reasons, including debugging, uh, and including a manufacturing test

claims.claim_text: Automated test racks that must exercise many target boards route each board's USB connection to a backplane and switch it through a matrix, so a single host can address any target under software control.
claims.quote_verbatim: all of the USB is exposed on that backplane that then could be switched
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: Peripheral combinations, not headline performance, often decide microcontroller selection: requiring Ethernet and high-speed USB on the same die eliminated most of the available high-end Cortex-M7 parts, leaving a choice between one part with extensive errata and one other family.
claims.quote_verbatim: you couldn't get Ethernet and high speed USB in the same silicon
claims.episode_title: Software Defined Power Supplies with Werner Johansson

claims.claim_text: An instrument powered only from a USB port and lacking a step-up converter is limited by the burden voltage drops in its own signal path: from a 5 volt input, the maximum usable output in its highest accuracy mode was 3.75 volts.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're USB powered in maximum accuracy mode, you can output up to 3.75 volts
claims.episode_title: Software Defined Power Supplies with Werner Johansson

claims.claim_text: The value of a host-connected instrument lies entirely in the conversion hardware between the physical signal and the bus; the bus itself contributes only a standard, universally available transport.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't just stick the antenna into your USB port. You need something in between
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Ettus - Quality Quadrature Quidam

claims.claim_text: Single-board computers have used one hub part with an internal port tied to an on-die Ethernet controller to provide both networking and multiple external USB ports; depopulating that part and linking the processor's USB straight to a single connector produces a cheaper, lower-power variant of the same board from the same bare PCB.
claims.quote_verbatim: which gives you, it's a three-port USB hub
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eben Upton - Morbus Moilsome MakerFaire

claims.claim_text: Emulating an Ethernet interface over USB lets a single cable supply power and a network connection to an embedded Linux board, which the host sees as a virtual network adapter it can address over the network stack it already has.
claims.quote_verbatim: They emulate Ethernet over USB
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, IndieGoGo & Ignite - Jasperated Jimswinger Jobbery

claims.claim_text: Presenting the board as a network device and serving a web page on it removes the need for terminal software or drivers on the host, at the cost of the connection being unfamiliar to users expecting a serial port.
claims.quote_verbatim: it shows up as a network device, like through USB
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Kridner and Robert Nelson

claims.claim_text: Reading a device's console on a phone or tablet over a single USB-C cable requires the target to implement serial-over-USB itself; the convenience is a property of the target's firmware, not of the cable.
claims.quote_verbatim: you would have to have support into the product that you're debugging to be able to send that serial stuff over the USB
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
